source.title: Emulated Disalignment: Safety Alignment for Large Language Models May Backfire!
source.authors: Zhan-Hui Zhou; Jie Liu; Zhichen Dong; Jia-Heng Liu; Chao Yang; Wan-Li Ouyang; Yu Qiao

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether an inference-time change to token sampling can increase harmful responses, using contrastive output distributions from aligned and pre-trained model pairs rather than fine-tuning, prefilling, or suffix attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper tests emulated disalignment (ED), a contrastive decoding attack, on harmful-user-query response rates. It does not test fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples, response-position KL concentration, compliant-prefix prefilling, adversarial suffixes, localized safety weights, or training intended to deepen safety. The synthetic experiments assess a learned preference-model safety score rather than harmful-response rates, so they are not rows for the tested version. Table 1 baselines are recorded as reference values in the ED rows. The paper also reports figure-only alpha and model-size trends; those are represented by aggregate rows only where the authors explicitly summarize the trend.
record.test_reason: ED is an inference-time decoding change: it contrasts the aligned model's token distribution with its base model's. It raises harmful-response rates on harmful queries well above the aligned models' own rates. This bears on V4's decoding-change clause. The attacked system is a base+aligned pair, not the aligned model alone, and ED acts at every position rather than only past the opening. The version-relevant comparison is therefore ED against AlignMP, the aligned model with a malicious system prompt. The record used BaseMP instead.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that ED reverses safety alignment at inference by contrasting aligned and pre-trained token distributions, with no training. It doubles pre-trained models' harmfulness and reaches the highest harmful rate in 43 of 48 subsets. They argue stronger alignment can backfire into greater misuse potential, and urge rethinking open release. Limits they note: it needs full output distributions and a shared vocabulary, and the token-level approximation fails for the safest models.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce few-example fine-tuning. It uses a training-free contrastive decoding distribution based on an aligned/base model pair and a malicious system prompt.
record.method_sensitivity: The harmful rate varies with alpha, model family, dataset, evaluator, query subset, model pairing, and prompting. The paper reports an initial increase and then decline as alpha rises; its evaluator tools can disagree on individual conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic DPO experiments on Anthropic-HH, safer aligned models (larger β⁻¹) yield more harmful ED models, except at the largest β⁻¹. Safety is measured by a learned reward-model score, not a harmful rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stronger alignment increases potential harm under emulated disalignment (alignment-reversal via contrastive decoding).

fits_no_version.finding: Safety-aligned models are essential: EDBase, which uses a benign-prompted base model instead, falls far short of ED. Few-shot malicious prompting further raises ED harmfulness (Figure 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The aligned/base log-ratio encodes a usable safety direction that can be inverted at inference.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (2024)
record.problems: The behavioral evaluation uses open-source model pairs with access to full token distributions and shared vocabularies; the authors note this limits applicability to proprietary models and unlike-vocabulary pairs. Main table values are means across five random seeds but provide no spread or confidence interval. Harmfulness assessments vary by evaluator. Alpha values were chosen by trial and error using fewer than 50 harmful queries devised by the authors, though they state these were not the evaluation datasets.
record.rows_left_out: No Table 1 rows were retained for safe-query subsets or for the other baselines (AlignMP and EDBase); these are not harmful-user-query response outcomes for the V4 rows above. Detailed plotted alpha values are figure-only and are summarized in r34 rather than transcribed panel by panel.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant start, adversarial suffixes, and whether the bypass acts via the opening tokens specifically. ED modifies every token position.
No test of what causes shallowness.

missing.what: AlignMP harmful-query rates (the aligned model's own rate under a malicious prompt), which are the correct V4 baselines for every Table 1 harmful-query row
Few-shot (1-shot, 5-shot) ED vs BaseMP harmful rates, averaged over datasets and query types

record.verdict_notes: The record's main error is using BaseMP as the baseline. That measures whether ED beats the malicious-prompted base model, which is the authors' framing. V4 instead asks whether a decoding change defeats the aligned model's refusal, so AlignMP is the relevant comparison. Under AlignMP, r5 is not reversed but r15 (Mistral) is. ED combines base and aligned models at every token, so it says nothing about the 'opening tokens' mechanism. Harmful rates come from moderation classifiers, not refusal or compliance judgments.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples, and no test of whether such training removes refusal.
No fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data.
No per-token KL measurement or analysis of aligned-versus-base differences by response position.
Tests ED's contrastive decoding manipulation, not compliant-opening prefills or adversarial suffixes; it does not test decoding changes other than ED.
No weight or rank localization or editing experiment.
Does not test whether training data or objectives cause safety to be shallow in the first response tokens.
No training method intended to spread safety beyond the first tokens, or test of such a method's robustness.
